extracted.intended_audience: researchers and graduate students in health psychology, positive psychology, behavioral medicine, and epidemiology
extracted.subtask_description: A meta-analytic research synthesis that evaluates how positive psychological constructs (subjective well-being, positive affect, optimism) affect objective physical and physiological health outcomes, and which moderators (e.g., outcome type, baseline health, age, gender, operationalization) influence those effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining well-being (SWB)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjective well-being (SWB) used as an overarching term comprising happiness, life satisfaction, and positive affect; includes emotional responses (frequent positive, infrequent negative moods) and global judgments of life satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use SWB to encompass measures of positive affect, life satisfaction, optimism, and related positive psychological constructs; treat these as separable but highly correlated constructs that often form a single higher-order factor (citations: Diener, Watson & Clark, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining ill-being
rubrics_metrics.description: Ill-being refers to negative psychological constructs that are measured (e.g., negative moods, stress, anger, depression) or manipulated (negative emotion inductions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studies report both well-being and ill-being relations with health, compute and compare effect sizes separately to assess unique contributions and similarities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operationalizing well-being: trait vs. state
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-being can be operationalized as trait (long-term happiness/optimism) or state (transient emotions/moods induced or sampled).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose measures appropriate to the research design: longitudinal studies typically use trait measures (e.g., SWLS, LOT), ambulatory and experimental studies use state measures (PANAS, Affect Balance, POMS) or manipulations (films, imagery, music, Velten task). Expect different relations with short- vs long-term health outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring well-being: self-report acceptability and convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-report measures are appropriate for well-being because the 'final judge' is subjective; such measures converge with informant reports, behavioral observations (smiling), recall, and physiological responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although self-reports are subjective, their convergence with other indicators justifies their use; include instruments like SWLS, PANAS, Affect Balance Scale, Profile of Mood States, and consider manipulations for experimental work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining health (holistic/process framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Health is defined not only as a state (lack of disease, normal function) but also as a lifelong process of regulation across autonomic, neuroendocrine, and immune systems; this meta-analysis adopts the holistic/process perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize health to capture both momentary system functioning and long-term regulation; consider health as maintenance of normal functioning and symptom control for chronic illness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer objective health outcomes over subjective reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Health should be operationalized in terms of physiological measures and relatively objective physical outcomes rather than relying on subjective self-reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective measures reduce shared method variance with well-being self-reports and are valuable for public health implications (e.g., extending life expectancy); include molecular and molar markers (hormones, immune markers, cardiovascular measures, longevity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion criteria for study designs
rubrics_metrics.description: Include experimental, ambulatory (experience sampling), and longitudinal studies in analyses; exclude cross-sectional/correlational studies when assessing directional influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These designs provide stronger evidence for causal direction (experiments manipulate affect; ambulatory captures within-person changes; longitudinal assesses whether prior well-being predicts future health).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of non-hedonic QOL measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude specific non-hedonic quality-of-life (QOL) measures that focus primarily on physical symptoms and medical issues (e.g., QLQ-30, FACT), because they are not measures of emotional responses or global life satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat disease-focused QOL instruments as proxies for well-being when the construct of interest is subjective well-being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of health outcomes (three-level taxonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify health outcomes into three broad types: short-term outcomes, long-term outcomes, and disease/symptom control for chronically ill samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to organize analyses and moderator tests; it reflects both length of follow-up and initial health status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twelve specific health outcome groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Break the three broad categories into 12 groups: Short-term — (a) immune system response, (b) cardiovascular reactivity, (c) endocrine functioning/response, (d) physiological response, (e) pain tolerance. Long-term — (a) general health outcomes, (b) cardiovascular functioning, (c) respiratory functioning, (d) longevity. Disease/symptom control — (a) respiratory control (e.g., asthma/allergies), (b) disease progression, (c) survival with terminal conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each group comprises various specific markers; analyze effects separately by group to detect differential relations between well-being and specific physiological/clinical outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markers of immune functioning (molecular markers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Markers include increases in lymphocytes (T cell counts: CD4, CD8, CD16), leukocytes (NK cells, macrophages, interleukins), and immunoglobulins (e.g., sIgA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these markers to index normal immune responses to challenges or vaccines; combine multiple immune markers where informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markers of autonomic/endocrine/physiological reactivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Markers of stress activation include cortisol, epinephrine/adrenaline, heart rate, blood pressure, finger temperature, and skin conductance; normal responses should return to baseline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess both magnitude of reactivity and recovery; non-normal sustained responses may indicate dysregulation linked to poorer health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Molar-level physiological markers and fitness
rubrics_metrics.description: Molar indicators include cardiovascular strength (power output, flow rates), cholesterol ratio, body weight, expiratory volume, peak expiratory flow, oxygen saturation, and longevity (verified via vital records).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are longer-term, functional indicators of health and fitness; include in analyses of long-term outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disease and symptom-control measures for chronic illness
rubrics_metrics.description: For chronic conditions, outcome measures focus on symptom control and functional maintenance (e.g., skin test wheal/flare sizes for allergies, measures of respiratory function in asthma, disease progression metrics, survival despite terminal illness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select markers appropriate to the disease context and interpret improvements as increased symptom control or stable functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Health outcome as a moderator
rubrics_metrics.description: The type of health outcome moderates the well-being–health relation: well-being is expected to increase health-related functioning (longevity, pain tolerance), improve ANS and immune functioning, and buffer/reduce reactivity and disease progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect stronger effects for short-term outcomes (immediate physiological responses) than for long-term outcomes, where many intervening variables can attenuate effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline health as a moderator
rubrics_metrics.description: Baseline health status (healthy vs. unhealthy samples) moderates effects: well-being is expected to have greater effects in unhealthy/dysregulated samples than healthy ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider initial allostatic load and dysregulation when interpreting effect sizes; unhealthy samples may show larger, clearer changes or symptom control benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age as a moderator
rubrics_metrics.description: Sample age moderates effects because immune and physiological systems change with age; well-being may have stronger effects in older samples where health decline is more likely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When health decline is possible, changes are more evident; analyze age strata or include age as a moderator variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender as a moderator
rubrics_metrics.description: Gender may influence the role of well-being: predicted that well-being could be more important for males (acting as a buffer against decline), given gender differences in longevity and morbidity patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include gender composition as a moderator and interpret within the context of physiological and psychosocial sex differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: State manipulations and experimental methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental manipulations of transient emotion (films, imagery, music, Velten task) are appropriate for testing immediate effects of positive and negative affect on concurrent objective health outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use validated inductions; compare induced well-being vs induced ill-being to test salutary vs detrimental effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambulatory (experience sampling) methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambulatory designs use repeated daily/weekly assessments of affect (e.g., PANAS, Affect Balance) and link within-person mood fluctuations to short-term physiological outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate for tracking small changes over time and linking state affect to concurrent physiological markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine multiple physiological markers across systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Because body systems interact, combine multiple markers (e.g., heart rate, blood pressure, cortisol, immune markers) to assess system-level functioning and dysregulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although complex, integrated analyses can reveal parallel stories across systems; use multi-marker approaches when feasible and interpret holistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid shared-method variance
rubrics_metrics.description: Shared method variance between self-reported well-being and self-reported health can inflate associations; therefore emphasize objective physiological measures to test the well-being–health link.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer objective markers (biomarkers, clinical outcomes, survival) over subjective health reports when assessing directional influence of well-being on health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive expectations and comparative tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses include that well-being will positively relate to immune response and pain tolerance, may not significantly relate to cardiovascular/physiological reactivity, and that experimental inductions of well-being produce salutary effects whereas inductions of ill-being produce compromised health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these expectations to plan moderator analyses and to compare effect sizes across outcome types and study designs.
